kurals.tamil:
ஆகூழால் தோன்றும் அசைவின்மை கைப்பொருள்
போகூழால் தோன்றும் மடி.
kurals.transliteration:
Aakoozhaal thondrum asaivinmai kaipporul
Pokoozhaal thondrum madi.
kurals.meaning: When fate is set on bringing wealth, it gives rise to tireless effort; when fate is set on taking wealth away, it gives rise to laziness.
kurals.elementary: Imagine two kids with the same homework. One suddenly feels full of energy and finishes it; the other feels sleepy and gives up. This kural says that even the energy or the sleepiness you feel can be part of your fate: good fortune shows up as hard work, and bad fortune shows up as laziness.
kurals.university: Valluvar opens the chapter with a subtle psychological claim: fate (ஊழ், uzh) does not merely deliver outcomes from outside but works through the agent’s own dispositions. ஆகூழ் (aakuzh, ‘fate of gaining’) manifests as அசைவின்மை (unflagging perseverance), while போகூழ் (pokuzh, ‘fate of losing’) manifests as மடி (sloth). This neatly reconciles the chapter with the Kural’s many praises of effort elsewhere (e.g. the later chapters on ஆள்வினையுடைமை): effort is praised, yet the very capacity to make effort is itself read as a sign of a favourable destiny. Commentators such as Parimelazhagar treat ஊழ் as the ripened fruit of past deeds (பழவினை), which makes the idea closer to karmic causation than to arbitrary luck. The structure anticipates the Stoic ‘co-fated’ reply to the Lazy Argument: outcome and effort are fated together, so fatalism is no excuse for idleness.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The body, the doer (soul), the various senses, the many kinds of efforts, and Divine Providence—these are the five factors of action.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna lists five causes behind every action; human effort is one of them, but daiva (Providence or fate) is named as the decisive fifth.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, the Gita places effort and fate side by side: effort is real, but it operates inside a larger, destined frame.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong conceptual match (daiva + effort as joint causes); does not specifically say fate produces effort or sloth.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For it is God which worketh in you both to will and to do of his good pleasure.”
christianity.explanation: Paul tells believers that even their wanting to act and their actual doing are worked in them by God.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural says fate shows up as inner energy; Paul says the very will to act is given from above.
christianity._accuracy_note: Shares the idea that motivation itself is given from beyond the self; Paul speaks of grace, not fortune or wealth.

islam.quote_or_event: “As for he who gives and fears Allāh and believes in the best [reward], We will ease him toward ease. But as for he who withholds and considers himself free of need and denies the best [reward], We will ease him toward difficulty.”
islam.explanation: God ‘eases’ each person along the path matching their disposition, making one path smooth and the other hard.
islam.tie_back: Both texts describe a higher power smoothing a person’s road toward either flourishing or decline.
islam._accuracy_note: Close structural parallel (divinely eased paths to gain or loss), though the Qur'an ties the easing to prior moral choice.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Talmud teaches that everything is in the hands of Heaven except the fear of Heaven.
judaism.explanation: The Sages hold that circumstances such as wealth and fortune are set by Heaven, while a person’s reverence and moral choice remain their own.
judaism.tie_back: A partial contrast: the Kural puts even effort and sloth under fate, whereas the Talmud keeps inner moral choice outside it.
judaism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase. Agrees that fortune is decreed but deliberately exempts moral will, a useful contrast.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha rejects the view that whatever a person experiences is entirely caused by what was done in the past, arguing that such a view would leave no room for desire, effort, or the sense of what should and should not be done.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha argues that pure past-action determinism destroys the motivation to act rightly now, so he rejects it.
buddhism.tie_back: A deliberate contrast: the Kural lets fate produce effort or sloth, while the Buddha refuses to let past karma explain away present effort.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Contrastive entry: Buddhism rejects strict determinism (the view of Makkhali Gosala and others).

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Hesiod describes the three Moirai, Clotho, Lachesis and Atropos, as the powers who give mortals at their birth both good and evil to have.
greek_mythology.explanation: In Greek myth, each person’s share (moira) of good and bad is spun and allotted at birth.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like ஆகூழ் and போகூழ், the Moirai hand out a lot of gain or loss before any effort is made.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase. Shares the idea of an allotted portion of good and ill; says nothing of effort or sloth.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Cicero reports the ‘Lazy Argument’: if recovering from illness is fated, calling the doctor is pointless. Chrysippus answered that some events are ‘co-fated’: recovery and calling the doctor are fated together.
philosophy.explanation: The Stoics held that fate works through human actions, not around them, so fate is no excuse for doing nothing.
philosophy.tie_back: Valluvar makes the same move: fate comes to pass through effort (or through its absence).
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase. Strong philosophical parallel: effort and outcome are fated together.

kurals.tamil:
பேதைப் படுக்கும் இழவூழ் அறிவகற்றும்
ஆகலூழ் உற்றக் கடை.
kurals.transliteration:
Pedhaip padukkum izhavoozh arivagatrum
Aagaloozh utrak kadai.
kurals.meaning: A fate of loss makes even a clever person act foolishly, while a fate of gain, when it arrives, widens a person’s understanding.
kurals.elementary: Have you ever had a day when you kept making silly mistakes, and another day when every answer just clicked? This kural says bad fortune can make even smart people act silly, and good fortune can make people seem wiser than usual.
kurals.university: The couplet extends the previous one from will to intellect: இழவூழ் (izhavuzh, ‘the fate of loss’) makes one பேதை (a fool), while ஆகலூழ் (aagaluzh, ‘the fate of increase’) அறிவு அகற்றும், widening or enlarging understanding. Parimelazhagar and Mu. Varadarasan read அகற்றும் as ‘to expand’, not ‘to remove’. The idea is that judgement itself is vulnerable to fortune: brilliant people make ruinous decisions when their luck is turning. The same intuition appears across cultures as the sense that those heading for ruin are first robbed of good judgement, and in the biblical account of Ahithophel’s wise counsel being ‘defeated’ by divine design. Philosophically, it raises the question of moral luck: how far our rationality depends on circumstances we do not control.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Krishna traces a downward chain: attachment breeds desire, desire breeds anger, anger breeds delusion, delusion bewilders memory, and when memory is bewildered intelligence is lost and one falls.
hinduism.explanation: The Gita shows how a person’s intelligence (buddhi) can be lost step by step, leading to ruin.
hinduism.tie_back: Both describe a loss of reason that comes before a fall, though the Gita blames passion rather than fate.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase. Shares the ‘ruin through loss of intelligence’ pattern; the cause is desire, not destiny.

christianity.quote_or_event: “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and will bring to nothing the understanding of the prudent.”
christianity.explanation: Paul, quoting Isaiah, says God can overturn human cleverness whenever He chooses.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural says a fate of loss makes the wise foolish; here a higher power voids the understanding of the prudent.
christianity._accuracy_note: Matches the ‘wisdom undone from above’ half; Paul’s context is the gospel, not fortune.

islam.quote_or_event: “He gives wisdom to whom He wills, and whoever has been given wisdom has certainly been given much good.”
islam.explanation: Wisdom is described as a gift God grants to whomever He chooses.
islam.tie_back: Matches the second half of the Kural: a favourable decree enlarges understanding.
islam._accuracy_note: Covers the ‘gain-fate widens wisdom’ half only.

judaism.quote_or_event: “For the LORD had appointed to defeat the good counsel of Ahithophel, to the intent that the LORD might bring evil upon Absalom.”
judaism.explanation: Absalom rejects the sound advice of Ahithophel for worse advice because God has decreed his downfall.
judaism.tie_back: A near-perfect narrative example: a ruler bound for loss is led to choose foolishly.
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong match: judgement is overturned to bring about a decreed fall.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “To his own ruin the fool gains knowledge, for it cleaves his head and destroys his innate goodness.”
buddhism.explanation: In the wrong person, knowledge itself becomes a tool of self-destruction.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts see that intelligence can end in ruin, though the Dhammapada blames character rather than fate.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Weak-to-moderate: shares ‘knowledge leading to ruin’, with no doctrine of fate.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The chorus in Sophocles’ Antigone sings that evil comes to seem good to the one whose mind a god is leading toward ruin.
greek_mythology.explanation: Greek tragedy often shows ruin arriving through a god-sent blindness of judgement (atē).
greek_mythology.tie_back: The same pattern as இழவூழ் making a person foolish: judgement fails first, then fortune follows.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase. Strong match for the first half (divinely induced folly before a fall).

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the Myth of Er, the soul that draws the first lot hastily chooses the life of a great tyrant through folly and greed, and only later discovers that it includes the fate of devouring his own children.
philosophy.explanation: Plato shows how a lack of wisdom at the decisive moment locks a soul into a disastrous destiny.
philosophy.tie_back: Folly and ruin travel together in both texts, though Plato stresses the soul’s own responsibility.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase. Links folly with a ruinous lot; Plato makes the chooser responsible.

kurals.tamil:
நுண்ணிய நூல்பல கற்பினும் மற்றுந்தன்
உண்மை யறிவே மிகும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Nunniya noolpala karpinum matrundhan
Unmai yarive migum.
kurals.meaning: However many subtle books a person studies, in the end it is the understanding that is truly their own, the portion allotted by fate, that prevails.
kurals.elementary: You can give a pencil to every child in class, but each one will still draw in their own way. This kural says that reading many clever books helps, but in the end a person’s own natural understanding decides how they really think and act.
kurals.university: The key phrase is உண்மை அறிவு (unmai arivu): literally ‘the knowledge that truly is’ one’s own, which commentators gloss as the understanding given by ஊழ், as opposed to what is acquired from books (நூல்). Valluvar is not dismissing learning; he devotes whole chapters to கல்வி (learning). He is noting that learning is filtered through an innate capacity it cannot fully override. The Gita makes a parallel claim that even the learned act according to their own nature (prakṛti), and Heraclitus’ fragment that character is a person’s daimon points the same way. Modern debates on nature versus nurture, and on the limits of education, are a secular version of the same observation.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Even a man of knowledge acts according to his own nature, for everyone follows the nature he has acquired from the three modes. What can repression accomplish?”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna says that learning does not override the nature (prakṛti) a person has acquired.
hinduism.tie_back: Almost the same claim as the Kural: however learned, a person’s own innate nature wins out.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Very close match: innate nature prevails over acquired knowledge.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For to one is given by the Spirit the word of wisdom; to another the word of knowledge by the same Spirit … dividing to every man severally as he will.”
christianity.explanation: Paul teaches that wisdom and knowledge are distributed as gifts, each person receiving a different share.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural’s ‘own true understanding’, wisdom here is a given portion, not something merely studied into existence.
christianity._accuracy_note: Shares the ‘allotted wisdom’ idea; says nothing about book-learning failing to override it.

islam.quote_or_event: “We raise in degrees whom We will, but over every possessor of knowledge is one [more] knowing.”
islam.explanation: Degrees of knowledge are raised by God’s will, and no one’s learning is final.
islam.tie_back: Knowledge levels are set from above, which echoes the Kural’s view that one’s true understanding is allotted.
islam._accuracy_note: Moderate: divine allotment of knowledge; no contrast with book-learning.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Talmud relates that the angel appointed over conception brings the drop before God and asks whether it will become strong or weak, wise or foolish, rich or poor, but does not ask whether it will be righteous or wicked.
judaism.explanation: Wisdom, strength and wealth are fixed before birth; only moral character is left to free choice.
judaism.tie_back: It directly supports the Kural: wisdom (or foolishness) is set before any study begins.
judaism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase. Strong match on innate wisdom as pre-decreed.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Though all his life a fool associates with a wise man, he no more comprehends the Truth than a spoon tastes the flavor of the soup.”
buddhism.explanation: Being around wisdom does not give understanding to someone who lacks the capacity for it.
buddhism.tie_back: Exposure to wisdom, like reading many books, cannot replace the understanding that is truly one’s own.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Good match on the limits of external learning; Buddhism attributes capacity to kamma, not fixed fate.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Aeschylus’ Prometheus Bound, Prometheus, the giver of all human arts, admits that craft is far weaker than Necessity, and says Necessity is steered by the three Fates and the Furies.
greek_mythology.explanation: Even the god of forethought and skill cannot out-think what is fated.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Learning and skill, however subtle, are weaker than the portion fate assigns, which is the Kural’s point.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase. Skill-versus-necessity theme matches well; the context is cosmic, not individual intellect.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Heraclitus’ fragment ‘ēthos anthrōpōi daimōn’ is usually rendered ‘character is a person’s destiny’.
philosophy.explanation: A person’s inner character, not outside instruction, is what shapes their fate.
philosophy.tie_back: Both put a person’s inner, given nature above what is learned from outside.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase and gloss; Heraclitus makes character the fate, whereas Valluvar makes fate shape character.

kurals.tamil:
இருவேறு உலகத்து இயற்கை திருவேறு
தெள்ளிய ராதலும் வேறு.
kurals.transliteration:
Iruveru ulagaththu iyarkai thiruveru
Thelliya raadhalum veru.
kurals.meaning: Fate works in the world in two different ways: becoming wealthy is one thing, and becoming wise is quite another.
kurals.elementary: Some kids are great at sports and others are great at math, and being good at one doesn’t make you good at the other. This kural says money and wisdom work the same way: being rich and being wise come from different kinds of luck, so one doesn’t guarantee the other.
kurals.university: The couplet makes an observation anyone can check: wealth (திரு, thiru, also the name of the goddess of fortune) and clear wisdom (தெள்ளியர் ஆதல்) are handed out on separate tracks. The rich are often not wise, and the wise are often not rich. Commentators read இருவேறு இயற்கை as two distinct operations of ஊழ். Indian folk tradition expresses the same idea as the old rivalry between Lakshmi (wealth) and Saraswati (learning). Ecclesiastes’ remark that bread is not always to the wise nor riches to the understanding, the Talmudic teaching on sustenance depending on mazal rather than merit, and Aristotle’s puzzle about fortunate fools all record the same gap between intelligence and worldly reward.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Among women I am fame, fortune, fine speech, memory, intelligence, steadfastness and patience.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna lists fortune (śrī) and intelligence (medhā) as separate divine manifestations.
hinduism.tie_back: Wealth and wisdom appear as distinct gifts, matching the Kural’s ‘two different natures’.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Weak: lists fortune and intelligence as separate powers but does not contrast them. Best available Gita verse.

christianity.quote_or_event: “The race is not to the swift, nor the battle to the strong, neither yet bread to the wise, nor yet riches to men of understanding, nor yet favour to men of skill; but time and chance happeneth to them all.”
christianity.explanation: The Preacher notes that wisdom and understanding do not guarantee bread or riches.
christianity.tie_back: An almost exact match: riches and wisdom are separate lots, and one does not bring the other.
christianity._accuracy_note: Near-direct parallel on wisdom not bringing wealth; Ecclesiastes credits ‘time and chance’ rather than a fixed fate.

islam.quote_or_event: “It is We who have apportioned among them their livelihood in the life of this world and have raised some of them above others in degrees [of rank].”
islam.explanation: God Himself apportions people’s livelihoods and ranks.
islam.tie_back: Worldly wealth is a separately apportioned lot, as the Kural says.
islam._accuracy_note: Matches the idea of apportioned wealth; does not contrast it with wisdom (compare 2:269 on wisdom).

judaism.quote_or_event: Rava teaches that life, children and sustenance depend not on merit but on mazal (fortune). The Talmud illustrates this with two righteous sages, Rabba and Rav Ḥisda: one household enjoyed plenty while the other struggled for bread.
judaism.explanation: Equal virtue and learning did not produce equal prosperity, because sustenance follows fortune.
judaism.tie_back: A vivid illustration of the Kural: being wise and being rich are separate lots.
judaism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase. Very strong match: equally wise sages with unequal wealth.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Shorter Exposition of Kamma, the Buddha explains that beings are owners and heirs of their kamma, and that kamma is what separates beings into rich and poor, and into wise and foolish, each through its own specific causes.
buddhism.explanation: Wealth comes from one kind of past action (generosity) and wisdom from another (inquiry), so the two are distributed separately.
buddhism.tie_back: Close to the Kural: wealth and wisdom come from two different workings of past deeds.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase. Strong structural match: separate causes for wealth and for wisdom.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the myth Protagoras tells, Epimetheus hands out distinct endowments to each creature: speed to some, strength to others. He runs out before reaching humans, so Prometheus steals craft-wisdom and fire for them.
greek_mythology.explanation: Gifts are handed out one at a time, and no creature receives everything.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural’s two separate operations of fate, endowments are allotted separately rather than all together.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase. Weak match: shows separate allotment of gifts, not wealth versus wisdom.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle observes that some foolish people succeed in many things where luck is in control, and asks whether good fortune (eutuchia) is a natural gift quite separate from practical wisdom.
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle notices that success often lands on the unwise, and he tries to explain luck as something other than intelligence.
philosophy.tie_back: The same observation as the Kural: fortune and wisdom run on different tracks.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase. Strong match on the observed split between good fortune and wisdom.

kurals.tamil:
நல்லவை எல்லாஅந் தீயவாம் தீயவும்
நல்லவாம் செல்வம் செயற்கு.
kurals.transliteration:
Nallavai ellaaan theeyavaam theeyavum
Nallavaam selvam seyarku.
kurals.meaning: In the pursuit of wealth, fate can turn every favourable circumstance into an unfavourable one, and every unfavourable circumstance into a favourable one.
kurals.elementary: Sometimes you plan a picnic on a sunny day and it rains anyway. Other times you get stuck indoors and end up finding something wonderful. This kural says that when it comes to making money, luck can flip good chances into bad ones and bad chances into good ones.
kurals.university: Commentators take நல்லவை and தீயவை here as circumstances favourable or unfavourable to earning, such as the right time, place, means and partners, rather than moral good and evil. Solomon Pappaiah glosses the kural this way: even with the right time, place and trade, an adverse fate brings loss, and even without them a favourable fate brings profit. The couplet warns against over-confidence in planning, since the same conditions can produce opposite results depending on forces beyond calculation. Across traditions this becomes the theme of reversal: the Qur'an’s ‘perhaps you hate a thing and it is good for you’, Rabbi Akiva’s night journey, and Boethius’ turning wheel of Fortune.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “That which in the beginning may be just like poison but at the end is just like nectar and which awakens one to self-realization is said to be happiness in the mode of goodness.”
hinduism.explanation: The Gita notes that what feels bitter at first can prove sweet in the end, and the reverse.
hinduism.tie_back: It shares the Kural’s theme of reversal: things that seem bad can turn out good.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Weak: the reversal here is about spiritual discipline, not fortune in earning wealth.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And we know that all things work together for good to them that love God, to them who are the called according to his purpose.”
christianity.explanation: Paul assures believers that even apparent misfortunes are turned to good by God’s purpose.
christianity.tie_back: It matches the ‘bad becomes good’ half of the Kural under a higher governing power.
christianity._accuracy_note: Covers only the bad-to-good direction, and only for believers.

islam.quote_or_event: “But perhaps you hate a thing and it is good for you; and perhaps you love a thing and it is bad for you. And Allāh knows, while you know not.”
islam.explanation: Human judgements of good and bad can be reversed by what God alone knows.
islam.tie_back: An almost exact two-way match: the favourable can prove harmful and the unfavourable beneficial.
islam._accuracy_note: Very strong match: an explicit two-way reversal under divine knowledge.

judaism.quote_or_event: Rabbi Akiva, turned away from a town, sleeps in a field; wind blows out his lamp, a cat eats his rooster and a lion his donkey. That night an army captures the town, and his lack of light and noise saves him. He teaches that all the Merciful One does is for the good.
judaism.explanation: A string of misfortunes turns out to be what saved his life.
judaism.tie_back: Circumstances that looked disastrous turn out favourable, which is exactly the Kural’s reversal.
judaism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the narrative. Strong bad-to-good reversal; not specific to wealth.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “It may be well with the evil-doer as long as the evil ripens not. But when it does ripen, then the evil-doer sees (the painful results of) his evil deeds. It may be ill with the doer of good as long as the good ripens not. But when it does ripen, then the doer of good sees (the pleasant results of) his good deeds.”
buddhism.explanation: Present circumstances can be misleading, because the results of past action ripen later and may reverse them.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts describe good and bad conditions flipping because of a hidden force that ripens over time.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Good match on reversal through delayed ripening; the Buddhist cause is kamma, not an impersonal fate.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Croesus asks the Delphic oracle whether to attack Persia and is told that if he does he will destroy a great empire. Taking this as a promise, he attacks, and the empire he destroys is his own.
greek_mythology.explanation: What looked like the most favourable sign possible became the cause of his ruin.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Good omens and good conditions turn bad, the first half of the Kural in dramatic form.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Narrative paraphrase. A strong good-to-bad reversal involving a king’s wealth and power.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Lady Philosophy tells Boethius that Fortune turns her wheel without pause, and that adverse fortune is often more useful than prosperous fortune, because it reveals true friends and false goods.
philosophy.explanation: Boethius shows that good and bad fortune are always turning and can swap their value.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural, it says that favourable and unfavourable circumstances readily change places.
philosophy.source: Boethius, Consolation of Philosophy, Book II (Prose 1-2, 8)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase. A strong thematic match on the reversibility of fortune.

kurals.tamil:
பரியினும் ஆகாவாம் பாலல்ல உய்த்துச்
சொரியினும் போகா தம.
kurals.transliteration:
Pariyinum aagaavaam paalalla uyththuch
Choriyinum pogaa thama.
kurals.meaning: What fate has not made yours will not stay with you, however anxiously you guard it; and what fate has made yours will not leave you, even if you carry it off and throw it away.
kurals.elementary: Imagine holding sand tightly in your fist: it still slips out. Now imagine a boomerang: you throw it away and it comes back. This kural says things that aren’t meant for you slip away however hard you hold on, and things that are meant for you come back even if you throw them away.
kurals.university: The couplet turns on பால் (paal), ‘share’ or ‘portion’, the same word used for the three books of the Kural. Things outside one’s allotted share (பாலல்ல) cannot be kept even with painful guarding (பரியினும்), and things within it (தம) will not leave even if deliberately poured out (உய்த்துச் சொரியினும்). It is an extreme statement of possession as destiny. Greek tradition gives a near-perfect illustration in Polycrates’ ring, which was thrown into the sea and came back inside a fish. The ethical point, drawn out by Stoics like Epictetus, is that anxious clinging is irrational: one should hold possessions loosely, as things on loan.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “You have a right to perform your prescribed duty, but you are not entitled to the fruits of action.”
hinduism.explanation: The Gita teaches that results are not within a person’s control or ownership.
hinduism.tie_back: Both teach that what comes to you is not secured by grasping; results belong to a higher order.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Moderate: shares non-ownership of outcomes, but not the image of wealth leaving or returning.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Riches certainly make themselves wings; they fly away as an eagle toward heaven.”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs warns that wealth can simply vanish however much one fixes one’s eyes on it.
christianity.tie_back: It matches the first half of the Kural: riches not truly yours fly off despite careful watching.
christianity._accuracy_note: Covers only the ‘cannot be kept’ half.

islam.quote_or_event: “O Allāh, Owner of Sovereignty, You give sovereignty to whom You will and You take sovereignty away from whom You will.”
islam.explanation: Power and possession are given and taken by God, whatever the holder does.
islam.tie_back: Both say that keeping or losing possessions depends on a higher decree, not on the owner’s grip.
islam._accuracy_note: Good match on decreed giving and taking; concerns sovereignty more than personal wealth.

judaism.quote_or_event: “There is a sore evil which I have seen under the sun, namely, riches kept for the owners thereof to their hurt. But those riches perish by evil travail: and he begetteth a son, and there is nothing in his hand.”
judaism.explanation: Qoheleth describes carefully hoarded wealth that is lost anyway, leaving the heir with nothing.
judaism.tie_back: Close to the first half of the Kural: guarding wealth cannot keep what is not truly one’s portion.
judaism._accuracy_note: Good match on the ‘guarded wealth still perishes’ half.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “The fool worries, thinking, ‘I have sons, I have wealth.’ Indeed, when he himself is not his own, whence are sons, whence is wealth?”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha says the fool clings to possessions, not seeing that even the self is not truly owned.
buddhism.tie_back: Both expose the futility of anxious clinging to possessions.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Moderate: shares the critique of possessiveness; the Buddhist basis is non-self, not fate.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The tyrant Polycrates, warned that his luck was too perfect, throws his most treasured ring into the sea to ward off misfortune. Days later a fisherman brings him a large fish, and the ring is found inside it. His ally Amasis breaks off their friendship, sensing that Polycrates is doomed.
greek_mythology.explanation: What fate has assigned cannot be thrown away, and a doom that is fated cannot be bought off.
greek_mythology.tie_back: An almost literal picture of the second half of the Kural: what is yours comes back even when you throw it away.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Narrative paraphrase. A near-exact illustration of ‘thrown away, yet it will not go’.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Never say of anything, ‘I have lost it,’ but, ‘I have restored it.’”
philosophy.explanation: Epictetus teaches that possessions are only on loan and return to the one who gave them.
philosophy.tie_back: Both remove the anxiety of loss: what is not truly yours goes back, whatever you do.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Matches the ‘what is not your portion departs’ half; Stoic acceptance rather than a doctrine of allotted shares.

kurals.tamil:
வகுத்தான் வகுத்த வகையல்லால் கோடி
தொகுத்தார்க்கு துய்த்தல் அரிது.
kurals.transliteration:
Vaguththaan vaguththa vagaiyallaal kodi
Thoguththaarkku thuyththal aridhu.
kurals.meaning: Even those who amass crores of wealth can enjoy it only to the extent that the Ordainer has ordained; beyond that, enjoyment is impossible.
kurals.elementary: You could fill a whole room with candy, but if you have a toothache you can’t eat any of it. This kural says that piling up huge amounts of money doesn’t mean you’ll get to enjoy it; how much you actually enjoy is decided by fate.
kurals.university: The striking phrase வகுத்தான் வகுத்த வகை (‘the way apportioned by the Apportioner’) is one of the few places where Valluvar speaks of fate through an agent. Commentators differ on whether வகுத்தான் means God or the impersonal law of past deeds. The kural separates possession from enjoyment (துய்த்தல்): accumulation is within human reach, but the capacity to enjoy is allotted. The same gap appears in Ecclesiastes’ rich man to whom God does not give ‘power to eat thereof’, in Jesus’ parable of the rich fool, and in the myth of Midas starving amid gold. This makes the couplet a critique of hoarding as well as a statement about fate.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The opening verse of the Isha Upanishad teaches that all this is pervaded by the Lord, that one should enjoy through renunciation, and that one should not covet anyone’s wealth.
hinduism.explanation: True enjoyment comes only by accepting what is allotted by the Lord, not by grasping more.
hinduism.tie_back: Both tie enjoyment (bhoga/துய்த்தல்) to what is apportioned, not to what is accumulated.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase. Links rightful enjoyment to divine apportionment; does not speak of crores hoarded but unenjoyed.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Thou fool, this night thy soul shall be required of thee: then whose shall those things be, which thou hast provided?”
christianity.explanation: In the parable, a rich man plans to build bigger barns and enjoy his stores, but dies that very night.
christianity.tie_back: Wealth gathered is not wealth enjoyed; the decision lies with God, just as in the Kural.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong match: accumulated wealth cannot be enjoyed beyond what God allows.

islam.quote_or_event: Qārūn is given treasures whose keys alone would burden a band of strong men. He boasts that he earned them by his own knowledge, and the earth swallows him with his home. Onlookers then exclaim that Allāh extends provision to whom He wills and restricts it.
islam.explanation: Enormous wealth could not protect Qārūn or be enjoyed, because it was not his by divine allotment.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it shows that hoarded riches are enjoyed only as far as the Apportioner allows.
islam._accuracy_note: Narrative paraphrase. A strong match on vast hoarded wealth not being enjoyed.

judaism.quote_or_event: “A man to whom God hath given riches, wealth, and honour, so that he wanteth nothing for his soul of all that he desireth, yet God giveth him not power to eat thereof, but a stranger eateth it.”
judaism.explanation: Qoheleth describes a man with all the wealth he wants but without God-given power to enjoy it.
judaism.tie_back: Almost the Kural itself: possession without the allotted power to enjoy.
judaism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match: wealth held, enjoyment withheld by divine allotment.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “There is no satisfying sensual desires, even with the rain of gold coins.”
buddhism.explanation: Even a shower of gold cannot bring real satisfaction to a craving mind.
buddhism.tie_back: Both separate the amount of wealth from the enjoyment actually obtained.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Moderate: blames craving rather than fate for the lack of enjoyment.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: King Midas asks Dionysus that everything he touches turn to gold. His bread and wine harden into gold in his mouth, and he begs to be freed from the gift.
greek_mythology.explanation: Limitless gold becomes a curse because he cannot actually enjoy anything.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The most vivid picture of the Kural: endless wealth, yet enjoyment is impossible.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Narrative paraphrase. A strong match on wealth without enjoyment; the cause is his own wish rather than fate.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Seneca writes to Lucilius that the poor man is not the one who has too little, but the one who craves more.
philosophy.explanation: Wealth is measured by contentment, not by the size of one’s store.
philosophy.tie_back: Both deny that heaping up riches secures their enjoyment.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase. Weak on fate; shares the gap between accumulation and enjoyment.

kurals.tamil:
துறப்பார்மன் துப்புர வில்லார் உறற்பால
ஊட்டா கழியு மெனின்.
kurals.transliteration:
Thurappaarman thuppura villaar urarpaala
Oottaa kazhiyu menin.
kurals.meaning: The destitute, who have nothing to enjoy, would renounce the world, if only fate let the sufferings destined for them pass without making them undergo them.
kurals.elementary: Imagine someone with an empty lunchbox. You might think it would be easy for them to say ‘I don’t need lunch.’ But they still feel hungry. This kural says poor people would give up wanting things and become monks, but fate still makes them feel the troubles they are meant to go through, so they can’t let go.
kurals.university: This is the chapter’s most compressed and most debated couplet. துப்புரவு (thuppuravu) means the means of enjoyment; those without it (the destitute) would seem to be natural renunciants, since they have nothing to give up. The particle மன் signals an unrealised possibility: they *would* renounce, *if* the sufferings that are theirs to experience (உறற்பால) passed away without being fed to them (ஊட்டா கழியும்). The implication is ironic: poverty does not automatically produce detachment, because fate still insists that its allotted pains be tasted. This fits the karmic principle, shared with Buddhism and Jainism, that ripened deeds must be experienced and cannot simply be skipped.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “One who has taken his birth is sure to die, and after death one is sure to take birth again. Therefore, in the unavoidable discharge of your duty, you should not lament.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna names certain things as aparihārya, unavoidable, and something that must simply be passed through.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts speak of experiences that cannot be skipped and must be undergone.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Moderate: shares ‘the unavoidable must be undergone’; not about poverty or renunciation.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Seeing his days are determined, the number of his months are with thee, thou hast appointed his bounds that he cannot pass.”
christianity.explanation: Job says each human life runs within limits God has fixed.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural’s ‘sufferings that are one’s portion’, Job’s troubles run within set bounds.
christianity._accuracy_note: Weak-to-moderate: shares appointed limits on life; no link to poverty or renunciation.

islam.quote_or_event: “Say, ‘Never will we be struck except by what Allāh has decreed for us; He is our protector.’ And upon Allāh let the believers rely.”
islam.explanation: Every affliction that reaches a person has already been decreed.
islam.tie_back: Both hold that the troubles meant for someone will reach them.
islam._accuracy_note: Good on decreed affliction; nothing on the poor and renunciation.

judaism.quote_or_event: “For against your will were you formed, against your will were you born, against your will you live, against your will you will die.”
judaism.explanation: The Mishnah reminds people that the basic course of life is imposed on them, not chosen.
judaism.tie_back: Both texts say a person cannot opt out of the experiences allotted to them.
judaism._accuracy_note: Moderate: shares the idea of unavoidable, imposed experience.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha states that intentional deeds that have been done and accumulated do not come to an end without their results being experienced, whether in this life or later.
buddhism.explanation: Ripened kamma must be lived through; it cannot be cancelled simply by wishing.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the very principle behind the Kural: the sufferings due to a person must be ‘fed’ to them before they pass.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase. Strong doctrinal match on results that must be experienced; the renunciation angle is absent.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Pandora lifts the lid of the jar, countless ills fly out to roam among mortals, and only Hope stays inside. Hesiod says there is no way to escape the will of Zeus.
greek_mythology.explanation: Troubles are released into human life by divine design and cannot be avoided.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Both portray sufferings as a destined portion that mortals cannot escape.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase. Weak: general unavoidable ills, nothing on poverty or renunciation.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Demand not that events should happen as you wish; but wish them to happen as they do happen, and you will go on well.”
philosophy.explanation: Epictetus teaches peace through accepting whatever comes rather than demanding escape from it.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural observes that the poor cannot reach detachment while fated sufferings press on them; Epictetus offers acceptance as the way through.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Weak-to-moderate: a complementary response rather than a parallel claim.

kurals.tamil:
நன்றாங்கால் நல்லவாக் காண்பவர் அன்றாங்கால்
அல்லற் படுவ தெவன்.
kurals.transliteration:
Nandraangaal nallavaak kaanbavar andraangaal
Allar paduva thevan.
kurals.meaning: Those who take good fortune happily as good when it comes, why should they be distressed when misfortune comes, since both arise from the same fate?
kurals.elementary: When you win a game you say ‘Yay, lucky me!’ So when you lose, why get so upset? Both winning and losing come from the same luck. This kural asks us to take the bad days as calmly as we enjoy the good ones.
kurals.university: The couplet is a rhetorical question with a Stoic edge. If good fortune (நன்று) and misfortune (அன்று) both come from ஊழ், then welcoming one and lamenting the other is inconsistent. Mu. Varadarasan glosses it as good deeds and evil deeds ripening, which ties the couplet to karmic reasoning. The ethical advice is equanimity (சமநிலை): accept both outcomes as coming from one source. It is closely echoed in Job’s reply to his wife, in the Mishnah’s rule to bless God for the bad as for the good, in the Gita’s teaching on bearing pleasure and pain alike, in the Buddha’s eight worldly conditions, and in Nietzsche’s amor fati.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “O son of Kuntī, the nonpermanent appearance of happiness and distress, and their disappearance in due course, are like the appearance and disappearance of winter and summer seasons … one must learn to tolerate them without being disturbed.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna compares joy and sorrow to seasons that come and go and should be borne calmly.
hinduism.tie_back: The same counsel as the Kural: take good and bad with equal composure.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong match on equanimity towards alternating fortune.

christianity.quote_or_event: “What? shall we receive good at the hand of God, and shall we not receive evil?”
christianity.explanation: Job refuses to curse God after catastrophe, reasoning that good and ill come from the same hand.
christianity.tie_back: Nearly word for word the Kural’s question: if you accept the good, why protest the bad?
christianity._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match in both logic and rhetorical form.

islam.quote_or_event: “No disaster strikes upon the earth or among yourselves except that it is in a register before We bring it into being … In order that you not despair over what has eluded you and not exult [in pride] over what He has given you.”
islam.explanation: Because both loss and gain are pre-recorded, believers should neither despair nor exult.
islam.tie_back: The same logic as the Kural: one decree governs gain and loss, so meet both evenly.
islam._accuracy_note: Very strong match: a shared decree leads to equanimity in both directions.

judaism.quote_or_event: “One is obligated to recite a blessing for the bad that befalls him just as he recites a blessing for the good that befalls him.”
judaism.explanation: Jewish law requires blessing God for misfortune as well as for good fortune.
judaism.tie_back: It puts the Kural’s question into practice: respond to bad as you would to good.
judaism._accuracy_note: Very strong match; framed as a religious obligation.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha names eight worldly conditions: gain and loss, fame and disrepute, praise and blame, pleasure and pain. They come to everyone, and the instructed disciple is neither carried away by the pleasant nor crushed by the unpleasant.
buddhism.explanation: Good and bad fortune are paired features of every life and should be met with the same composure.
buddhism.tie_back: A close parallel to the Kural’s challenge to meet misfortune as calmly as fortune.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase. Strong match on equanimity in gain and loss.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Achilles tells the grieving Priam that two jars stand on Zeus’ threshold, one of good gifts and one of evil. Zeus gives some men a mixture and others only evil, so mortals must endure what is given.
greek_mythology.explanation: Good and bad fortune are dispensed by the same god, so grief must be borne.
greek_mythology.tie_back: One source for both good and ill, and so a call to endure the bad: the same reasoning as the Kural.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase. A strong match on a single divine source of good and ill.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Nietzsche resolves to learn to see what is necessary in things as beautiful, and names this ‘amor fati’, love of fate: to be one day only a Yes-sayer.
philosophy.explanation: Rather than resenting misfortune, one should embrace the whole of what is fated.
philosophy.tie_back: It goes a step beyond the Kural: not just avoiding distress at misfortune but loving the fate that brings it.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase. Strong thematic kinship; more affirmative than Valluvar’s equanimity.

kurals.tamil:
ஊழிற் பெருவலி யாவுள மற்றொன்று
சூழினுந் தான்முந் துறும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Oozhir peruvali yaavula matrondru
Soozhinun thaanmun thurum.
kurals.meaning: What is mightier than fate? Even when a person devises another way to escape it, fate gets there first.
kurals.elementary: Imagine playing tag with someone who always knows which way you’ll run and is already waiting there. That’s how this kural describes fate: whatever clever path you choose to avoid it, fate is already there ahead of you.
kurals.university: The chapter, and with it the whole Book of Virtue (அறத்துப்பால்), ends on a rhetorical question: ஊழிற் பெருவலி யாவுள, ‘what is of greater strength than fate?’ The second line gives the reason: even if one plans (சூழினும்) another course, fate itself arrives first (தான் முந்துறும்). The positioning matters. After thirty-seven chapters on virtue, Valluvar closes by acknowledging the limits of human agency. Book 2 (Porul) then opens with vigorous chapters on effort, and later ones such as ஆள்வினையுடைமை (e.g. Kural 620) even assert that tireless striving can push fate aside. The tension is intended, and it mirrors the Stoic formula that fate leads the willing and drags the unwilling, as well as the Oedipus myth, in which the flight from prophecy is what fulfils it.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Under illusion you are now declining to act according to My direction. But, compelled by the work born of your own nature, you will act all the same, O son of Kuntī.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna tells Arjuna that his refusal to fight is futile; his own nature will drive him to it anyway.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it says that whatever path you choose instead, the destined course still overtakes you.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong match: attempted avoidance is overridden by what is bound to happen.

christianity.quote_or_event: “There are many devices in a man’s heart; nevertheless the counsel of the LORD, that shall stand.”
christianity.explanation: Whatever plans people make, God’s purpose is what finally prevails.
christianity.tie_back: It closely mirrors the Kural: human schemes (சூழினும்) are overtaken by a stronger decree.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong match: many human devices, one prevailing counsel.

islam.quote_or_event: “Wherever you may be, death will overtake you, even if you should be within towers of lofty construction.”
islam.explanation: No fortress or plan can keep off what God has decreed.
islam.tie_back: The decree ‘arrives first’ wherever one hides, just as fate does in the Kural.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong match on inescapability despite precautions; the example is death specifically.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Everything is foreseen yet freedom of choice is granted.”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Akiva holds together God’s total foreknowledge and genuine human free will.
judaism.tie_back: A contrastive entry: it agrees nothing escapes God’s knowledge but, unlike the Kural, keeps real room for choice.
judaism._accuracy_note: Partial and contrastive: affirms that all is foreseen and also that choice is free.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Neither in the sky nor in mid-ocean, nor by entering into mountain clefts, nowhere in the world is there a place where one may escape from the results of evil deeds.”
buddhism.explanation: No hiding place allows escape from the ripening of one’s past actions.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it says every attempt to escape is met by what is already on its way.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Strong match on inescapability; the force is kamma, which Buddhism does not treat as fixed fate.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Told by the Delphic oracle that he will kill his father and marry his mother, Oedipus flees Corinth to avoid it. On the road he kills a stranger, Laius, his real father, and in Thebes he marries the widowed queen, his mother.
greek_mythology.explanation: The very plan made to escape the prophecy is what brings it about.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The perfect illustration of the Kural: devise another way, and fate is there first.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Narrative paraphrase. A near one-to-one match: the attempt to escape fulfils the fate.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Seneca quotes Cleanthes’ prayer to Zeus and Destiny, whose closing thought is that the Fates lead the willing and drag the unwilling.
philosophy.explanation: The Stoics taught that fate will be fulfilled either way; one can only choose whether to go willingly.
philosophy.tie_back: Resistance does not change the destination, which is the Kural’s point about fate’s supremacy.
philosophy.source: Seneca, Moral Letters to Lucilius 107.10-11 (quoting Cleanthes)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase. A strong match on the supremacy of fate over resistance.
